newsitem.title: CHINA: China interest rate cut unlikely soon-economist.
newsitem.headline: China interest rate cut unlikely soon-economist.

text.p: China is unlikely to cut interest rates again before the end of the year despite a fall in inflation, a Chinese government economist said on Monday.
Wang Jian, a researcher at the State Planning Commission, also said China's currency could strengthen slightly if the nation's trade surplus widened.
"Interest rates are already low in comparison to previous levels," Wang told reporters at an investment seminar.
"Another cut does not seem likely to me," he said, adding that another small cut would probably not stimulate retail spending.
He said that a more important step would be to ease tight curbs on investment and ensure that the funds were put to use efficiently.

China has cut interest rates twice this year -- in May and in August -- as inflation eased. Retail price inflation was only five percent in September, well below the target of 10 percent for the full year. That compares with 14.8 percent for all of last year and a high of 21.7 percent in 1994.
Wang, who said he was expressing his personal views, added he believed that the most significant interest rate move this year was the April removal of a subsidy paid on new long-term deposits.
The subsidy, paid on top of normal bank interest rates for deposits of three or more years, had reached a high of 13.24 percent in December last year.
That had placed a huge strain on the nation's banking system as banks were unable to lend long-term funds at profitable interest rates.
The economist said that the nation's currency, the yuan, was likely to remain stable though a further rise in the trade surplus could send it slightly higher.
China had a surprisingly robust $3.2 billion trade surplus in September, bringing the surplus for the first nine months of the year to $8.19 billion.
The yuan is now trading at about 8.3 to one dollar.
